assessment.nobel_worthiness: Direct imaging of the shadow of a supermassive black hole is a discovery in the plain sense: strong-field gravity near a horizon-scale object, previously accessible only through theory and indirect inference, is now observed. Of great interest from a gravitation and black-hole perspective, and it constrains alternatives such as horizonless compact objects, though at modest precision.
assessment.attribution: Falcke proposed the shadow-imaging concept for Sgr A* and M87, Doeleman led the mm-VLBI technical development and the collaboration's observational campaigns, and Zensus built the European VLBI institutional base. The roughly 300-person collaboration makes a three-person configuration somewhat arbitrary, and I cannot independently verify the precise division of credit.
assessment.maturity: M87* (2019) and Sgr A* (2022) were imaged by independent targets and processing pipelines, with consistency with general relativity. Interpretation of the ring and the polarisation results is stable. Recognition is timely, with continued improvements still coming.
uncertainties: Credit within a very large collaboration is hard to allocate to three people.
Tests of GR from the shadow are limited by astrophysical modelling uncertainty and current resolution.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction of flat bands at a magic angle and the subsequent observation of correlated insulators and superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene opened an entirely new, tunable platform for strongly correlated physics. Original, clear, and with large downstream impact on moire materials.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the 2011 continuum-model prediction of the magic angle, and Jarillo-Herrero's group delivered the decisive 2018 experiments. This is a clean theory-plus-experiment triple, though other experimental groups (e.g. Dean and Young on related moire platforms) and the Cao/Fuhrer-style experimental authorship questions might complicate it.
assessment.maturity: Replicated independently by many groups across many moire systems. The mechanism of the superconductivity is still debated, but the discovery of the phenomena is secure. Timing seems right.
uncertainties: The origin of superconductivity in the magic-angle system remains unsettled.
Other experimental groups and other moire systems could be argued to merit a share of credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The observation of a Higgs-like boson in 2012 confirmed the mechanism of mass generation in the Standard Model and is arguably the central experimental event of modern particle physics. The prediction was honoured in 2013, so the experimental discovery is the remaining half of that story.
assessment.attribution: ATLAS and CMS were each built by thousands of people; the founding spokespersons and project leaders of each (Jenni, Della Negra, Virdee) are the natural individuals, but any three-name selection is a convention and underrepresents the accelerator and detector builders. I note that the Nobel statutes constrain this, and I cannot verify the internal history of each experiment.
assessment.maturity: Two independent experiments in 2012, with extensive subsequent measurements of couplings and spin-parity consistent with the Standard Model. Fully mature; the delay is about attribution rather than evidence.
uncertainties: Allocation of credit within two huge collaborations is intrinsically problematic.
Whether the committee considers the discovery sufficiently separate from the 2013 prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The detection of a diffuse flux of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos, with the 2018 association of a neutrino event with the blazar TXS 0506+056 and the later Galactic-plane evidence, opens a new window on cosmic-ray accelerators. It is a discovery with a clear observational signature in nature.
assessment.attribution: Halzen was the principal architect and scientific leader of IceCube and Spiering was a central figure in the early neutrino telescope programme and the collaboration. This gives a two-person prize; other contributors to the early design (and Baikal/AMANDA pioneers) may deserve consideration, but they are not in the supplied credit.
assessment.maturity: Diffuse flux confirmed repeatedly, with independent confirmations in analyses of different event topologies. Source identification is still partly emerging, with TXS 0506+056 at modest significance and NGC 1068 stronger.
uncertainties: Individual source associations are of limited statistical significance.
Credit across a very large collaboration and a long, multi-generation effort is partly unresolved.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal, reach fractional uncertainties around 1e-18 and have become the leading frequency standards, with applications to tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and potential redefinition of the second. Very high impact, though the immediate story is metrology rather than a new phenomenon.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and demonstrated the first strontium lattice clocks; Ye brought the clock to its highest precision and stability. A two-person configuration is clean, with a possible overlap with the thorium nuclear clock candidate that would favour awarding Ye once only.
assessment.maturity: Many independent groups across the world have realised lattice clocks with strontium, ytterbium and other species, and international comparisons agree. Fully mature.
uncertainties: Overlap in credit for Jun Ye with other precision-metrology candidates.
Whether the committee views this as a discovery or an instrument advance.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: WMAP measured the CMB anisotropies with precision sufficient to fix the age, geometry, composition and reionisation history of the universe, establishing the standard LambdaCDM model and constraining inflationary parameters. It is a clear, central observational result for cosmology.
assessment.attribution: Bennett was the PI, Page a key instrument scientist and Spergel the leading analyst and theorist of the results. Credit seems fairly well-defined, but the CMB field has already been recognised twice (COBE in 2006, Peebles in 2019), and Planck has supplanted much of the precision.
assessment.maturity: Superseded in precision by Planck but strongly confirmed. The interpretation is stable and mature; the question is whether it is distinct enough from earlier prizes.
uncertainties: Overlap with the earlier cosmology prizes could weigh against it.
WMAP and Planck together contribute to the modern constraints; priority for specific results is not purely WMAP's.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realise Hubbard-type models with exquisite control, as with the superfluid-to-Mott-insulator transition and quantum gas microscopes. They give new, clean access to many-body physics that is hard to reach in solids or numerically.
assessment.attribution: Zoller and Jaksch provided the theoretical proposal, Greiner and Bloch performed the Mott-insulator experiment and microscope work, and Esslinger the fermionic Hubbard realisations; a three-person selection excludes one of the central figures. Jaksch is not in the supplied credit.
assessment.maturity: Widely replicated and still growing, though 'simulation' of problems not yet solved by classical methods is still an evolving claim. Part of the field already has Nobel recognition through the 2001 and 2012 AMO prizes.
uncertainties: Genuine quantum advantage in simulation remains unproven.
A three-person limit forces exclusion of an important contributor.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Detection of the baryon acoustic peak in galaxy clustering gives a standard ruler that independently tests the cosmic expansion history and dark energy, relevant to the open question of the nature of dark energy. A clean, interpretable signal in nature that strengthens the case for LambdaCDM.
assessment.attribution: The 2005 detections came from SDSS (Eisenstein et al.) and 2dFGRS (Cole, Colless et al.); theoretical origins go back to Sunyaev and Zeldovich and to Peebles and Yu, so the credit is somewhat diffuse. I selected the observers of the first detections and cannot verify the full history.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by BOSS, eBOSS and now DESI; the technique is mature, though recent DESI hints about evolving dark energy are not settled. Recognition is plausible but possibly secondary to the 2011 prize.
uncertainties: Credit is split between observers and early theorists and across two surveys.
The 2011 prize on acceleration may reduce appetite for a second dark-energy-related award.
